newsitem.title: USA: Wall St seen opening lower on pre-election anxiety.
newsitem.headline: Wall St seen opening lower on pre-election anxiety.

text.p: U.S. stocks should open lower Monday as anxious investors stick to the sidelines, worried about a possible Democratic sweep of both houses of Congress in tomorrow's U.S. elections.
"It looks like a lower opening," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.
The 30-year benchmark Treasury bond was off 6/32, yielding 6.69 percent. Standard & Poor's December futures fell 0.35 to 706.15 ahead of Monday's opening.

Many observers expect President Clinton to be re-elected easily, and market analysts are turning their eyes to the congressional races and speculating about whether the Republicans will lose control of the House and Senate.
"It's going to be very cautious because if the Democrats take Congress, that would be very negative for the stock market," Cardillo said. "We could see a 10 to 15 percent drop if that happened."
At 1000 EST/1500 GMT the market will get a chance to digest September construction spending data, although the figures should take a back seat to the election jitters.
Analysts expect a fall of 0.1 percent, compared to a rise of 0.9 percent in August.
The Tokyo stock market was closed for a "culture day" holiday on Monday. Trading will resume on Tuesday. On Friday the Nikkei average 225 closed 166.20 points higher at 20,633.
In London the FTSE 100 Index was off 2.5 points at 3946.
The dollar was weaker in thin trading in Asia and hemmed into tight ranges in Europe by fears of a Democratic Congress.
In London, General Motors shares rose after news that workers at a key metal stamping plan in Indianapolis had begun returning to work.
The blockbuster merger between British Telecommunications Plc and MCI Communications Corp, announced over the weekend, could help merger stocks, Cardillo said.
The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column said Sears Roebuck and Co's earnings growth may have been smoothed by a 1993 credit card reserves balance-sheet maneuver.
